chapter_summary:
While `@State` and `@Binding` are excellent for managing simple, local value-type data, many real-world applications deal with more complex data structures, often represented by reference types (classes). SwiftUI provides a robust mechanism for observing changes in these reference types through the `ObservableObject` protocol, coupled with the `@ObservedObject` and `@StateObject` property wrappers.

At the heart of this system is the `ObservableObject` protocol. Any class that conforms to `ObservableObject` can be observed by SwiftUI views. To signal that a property within an `ObservableObject` has changed and that observing views should re-render, you must mark that property with the `@Published` property wrapper. When a `@Published` property changes, the `ObservableObject` automatically emits a notification, which SwiftUI intercepts to update the UI. This allows you to encapsulate your application's logic and data within classes, separating concerns from your view hierarchy. For instance, a `UserProfile` class might conform to `ObservableObject` and have `@Published var name: String` and `@Published var email: String`.

Now, let's look at how views interact with these `ObservableObject`s. The `@ObservedObject` property wrapper is used when a view needs to observe an `ObservableObject` that is *created and managed externally*. This means the `ObservableObject` instance is typically passed into the view from an ancestor view or an external data source. The view using `@ObservedObject` does not own the object; it merely observes it. If the view is re-created (e.g., due to its parent's state changing, or navigation stack popping and pushing), the `@ObservedObject` will be re-initialized with the same external instance, or a new one if the parent provides it. This is suitable when you have a long-lived data model that exists independently of a specific view's lifecycle.

However, a critical challenge arises when a view *needs to own* an `ObservableObject` instance. If you were to use `@ObservedObject` for an object created directly within a view (e.g., `init()`), that object would be re-created every time the view's `body` is re-evaluated or the view itself is re-initialized by SwiftUI. This leads to data loss and unexpected behavior. This is where `@StateObject` becomes indispensable.

The `@StateObject` property wrapper is designed for creating and *owning* an `ObservableObject` instance within a view's lifecycle. When you declare an `ObservableObject` with `@StateObject`, SwiftUI ensures that the object is created only once for that view and persists for the entire lifetime of the view. Even if the view's `body` is re-evaluated multiple times, or the view is temporarily removed and re-added to the hierarchy (e.g., within a `NavigationView` or `TabView`), the `@StateObject` instance remains the same, preserving its data. This makes `@StateObject` the correct choice when a view is responsible for initializing and managing its own complex data model.

Let's illustrate with an example. Suppose you have a `TimerManager` class that conforms to `ObservableObject` and has a `@Published var secondsElapsed: Int`. If your `ContentView` needs to create and manage this timer, you would declare it as `@StateObject var timer: TimerManager = TimerManager()`. This ensures that `timer` is created once when `ContentView` appears and persists as long as `ContentView` is alive. If `ContentView` then passes this `timer` instance to a child `TimerDisplayView`, the `TimerDisplayView` would declare it as `@ObservedObject var timer: TimerManager`. The child view observes the timer, but the parent `ContentView` owns it.

A common and critical mistake is using `@ObservedObject` when `@StateObject` is needed. If you declare `var timer: TimerManager = TimerManager()` and then use `@ObservedObject var timer: TimerManager` in the same view, every time the view updates, a *new* `TimerManager` instance will be created, resetting your timer. This is a subtle but profound difference that can cause significant headaches in debugging. Always remember: if a view needs to *create and own* an `ObservableObject` instance, use `@StateObject`. If it needs to *observe* an `ObservableObject` instance that is passed in or created elsewhere, use `@ObservedObject`.

Safety notes: When working with `ObservableObject`s, be mindful of strong reference cycles, especially if your `ObservableObject` holds references to views or other objects that might also hold references back to it. Use `[weak self]` or `[unowned self]` in closures within your `ObservableObject` where necessary to prevent memory leaks. Also, remember that `@Published` properties are for signaling changes. If you have complex logic that modifies multiple properties, you might need to explicitly call `objectWillChange.send()` before making changes and `objectWillChange.send()` again after, though `@Published` usually handles this for individual properties.

screens.title: Managing Complex Data with @ObservedObject and @StateObject
screens.subtitle: How SwiftUI observes reference-type models and why ownership matters

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how SwiftUI keeps views in sync with complex, reference-type data. We'll introduce the ObservableObject protocol and the @Published property wrapper so that your data model can announce changes. Then you'll see the two common wrappers views use to connect to those models: @ObservedObject, which watches objects created elsewhere, and @StateObject, which creates and owns an object for the life of a view. You will also see common pitfalls — especially the subtle bug where a view accidentally re-creates an object and loses state — and how to avoid that by choosing ownership intentionally. As a concrete orientation, we'll build a simple GameManager that publishes a score and show how a parent view can own it while a child view observes it. Knowing these patterns prevents surprising resets and lifecycle bugs in navigation and tab layouts. By the end you should be able to choose whether a view should observe a shared model or own a model it creates, and explain why that choice preserves state across view updates.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: ObservableObject + @Published notify views; use @StateObject to own and persist a model, and @ObservedObject to observe externally owned models.

narration.text: Over the next screens we'll focus on practical skills you can apply immediately. First, you will understand what an ObservableObject is and why reference types need explicit change notifications. Second, you'll implement the ObservableObject protocol in a class and use @Published to mark properties that should trigger UI updates. Third, you'll learn how to observe a model created elsewhere using @ObservedObject so multiple views can react to shared data. Finally, you'll practice owning and preserving a model inside a view using @StateObject so data survives view re-creation and navigation. Each objective includes a concrete scenario, like a GameManager tracking a score, and a small mnemonic to help you remember ownership versus observation. We'll also validate competency with a small milestone after the hands-on activity. These objectives are practical: by the end you'll know which property wrapper to pick and why, and you'll be able to avoid a common bug that resets class-based state when a view is re-rendered.

screens.title: What is ObservableObject and @Published?
screens.subtitle: Definition and concrete behavior for reference-type models

narration.text: ObservableObject is a protocol you add to a class so SwiftUI can listen for changes in that class's stored properties. The essential companion is @Published: apply it to properties whose changes should notify observing views. When a @Published property changes, the ObservableObject emits a change notification that SwiftUI uses to re-render views that observe the object. This makes a class behave like a reactive source of truth. A clear concrete example: a UserProfile class can conform to ObservableObject and expose @Published var name and @Published var email. When the name changes, any view observing the UserProfile will update automatically. A common misconception is to treat ObservableObject like @State. @State is for simple value types owned by the view; ObservableObject is for reference types and for situations where multiple views share one instance. Another subtle point: @Published usually handles sending notifications for simple property changes, but if you update multiple fields in a single operation you can call objectWillChange. send() to batch updates and avoid inconsistent intermediate renders. Takeaway: ObservableObject and @Published let classes broadcast state changes; use them when your data is a reference type and when multiple views need to react to the same instance.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: ObservableObject + @Published turn classes into reactive models that notify SwiftUI when their properties change.

content.html:
Definition
ObservableObject and @Published
Classes that conform to ObservableObject can notify views when marked fields change. Use @Published for the fields that should broadcast changes.
Concrete example
A UserProfile class with @Published name and email updates all observing views when either property changes.
Common misconception
ObservableObject is not a direct replacement for @State. It is for reference-type models that may be shared or owned by views.
Tip
If updating multiple properties, consider objectWillChange.send() to batch notifications and avoid multiple re-renders.
Example code
class UserProfile: ObservableObject {
  @Published var name: String = ""
  @Published var email: String = ""

  func update(name: String, email: String) {
    // For multiple updates, you can batch notifications if needed
    self.name = name
    self.email = email
  }
}
Key takeaway
Use ObservableObject for shared, class-based models and mark fields with @Published to notify views.
Watchout
Don’t confuse @State with ObservableObject—ownership and type semantics differ.

narration.text: Change propagation with ObservableObject follows a predictable flow that you can rely on when designing models. Step one: your class marks a property with @Published. Step two: that property changes at runtime — perhaps a fetch completes or the user updates a form. Step three: the @Published property automatically calls into the ObservableObject's change publisher, which emits an update. Step four: SwiftUI receives that emission and schedules the view body to re-evaluate, updating the UI to reflect the new state. A concrete example: a TimerManager has @Published secondsElapsed, and every timer tick increments that property; views observing the TimerManager get updated seconds displayed. A common pitfall is assuming notifications are instantaneous and synchronous; SwiftUI may schedule work on the main run loop to batch UI updates. Another misconception is relying on property observers like didSet to notify views — prefer @Published or objectWillChange. send() because property observers alone won't inform SwiftUI. Key takeaway: understand each step so you design models that emit changes correctly and avoid partial updates or redundant renders. How change propagation works means property marked @published changes → observableobject emits → swiftui schedules a re-render of observing views.. In practical terms, from @published updates to swiftui re-renders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Propagation steps
keyIdea.text: Property marked @Published changes → ObservableObject emits → SwiftUI schedules a re-render of observing views.

content.html:
Process Flow
Change propagation
Follow the chain from model change to UI update so you can predict and prevent update issues.
1. Mark properties
Add @Published to fields the UI should react to.
2. Update value
Change occurs from business logic, timers, or network callbacks.
3. Emit change
@Published emits via the ObservableObject's publisher to inform observers.
4. SwiftUI updates
Observing views re-evaluate their body and reflect the new state.
Concrete example
// TimerManager example
class TimerManager: ObservableObject {
  @Published var secondsElapsed: Int = 0
  // timer increments secondsElapsed every second
}
Misconception
Don't expect didSet to replace @Published. Use @Published or objectWillChange for SwiftUI-aware notifications.
Key takeaway
Rely on the @Published → ObservableObject → SwiftUI chain to update UI predictably.

narration.text: Choosing between @ObservedObject and @StateObject is a question of ownership. Use @ObservedObject when a view needs to observe a model created elsewhere and managed by a parent or global source. The view is a spectator: it reacts to changes but doesn’t control lifecycle. In contrast, @StateObject is for views that instantiate and own a model. SwiftUI creates the object once and preserves it across re-renders and temporary removals. A frequent bug arises when a view initializes an ObservableObject directly but uses @ObservedObject: the object is re-created every time the view is recreated, which resets state. For example, if you write @ObservedObject var timer = TimerManager() inside a view, the timer will restart when the view's body changes. The correct fix is @StateObject var timer = TimerManager() so the instance persists. Another nuance: a parent view should own a model using @StateObject if it must be shared with children; children should declare it as @ObservedObject. This pattern clearly signals ownership and prevents accidental reinitialization. Reflect on which view must preserve the data to decide ownership correctly. @ObservedObject vs @StateObject means if a view creates the observableobject, use @stateobject; if it receives it, use @observedobject.. In practical terms, ownership, lifecycle, and common bugs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ownership rule
keyIdea.text: If a view creates the ObservableObject, use @StateObject; if it receives it, use @ObservedObject.

content.html:
@ObservedObject
Observe external models
Used when a model is created and owned by a parent or external source. The view updates when the model changes but does not manage its lifecycle.
Use case
Child view displaying shared data from a parent-owned GameManager.
Common bug
Initializing an object inside the same view with @ObservedObject causes re-creation and state loss.
@StateObject
Create and own the model
Use when a view is responsible for instantiating an ObservableObject. SwiftUI ensures the object is only created once for the view's lifetime.
Use case
A ContentView that creates a GameManager to persist scores while the view is alive.
Fix for re-init bug
Replace @ObservedObject var manager = Manager() with @StateObject var manager = Manager() in the owning view.
Concrete scenario
Parent creates GameManager with @StateObject. Child receives it as @ObservedObject. If parent incorrectly used @ObservedObject to create it, the instance would be recreated when the parent re-renders, resetting game data.

screens.title: Owner/Observer architecture with GameManager
screens.subtitle: Parent owns model; children observe it

narration.text: An effective architecture pattern is for a parent view to own complex models while child views observe them. Consider a GameManager that tracks currentScore and gameName. The parent ContentView should create and own a GameManager using @StateObject. That guarantees the manager persists for as long as ContentView exists. Child views, like ScoreDisplayView, receive the same instance and declare it with @ObservedObject. They react to changes but do not manage initialization or deallocation. This separation of responsibilities keeps lifecycle predictable. Practically, when the parent toggles whether a child is shown, the GameManager remains intact because the parent owns it. If instead the child created the manager and used @ObservedObject, toggling the parent could recreate the manager and lose score. A concrete debugging technique is to add print statements in the manager's init and deinit to confirm ownership. Architecting models this way improves testability too: you can inject mock managers into child views without changing their code. Think of ownership as custody — the owner keeps the data alive and children borrow it to read and display state. Owner/Observer architecture with GameManager means parent views should own long-lived models with @stateobject; child views observe them with @observedobject to stay in sync.. In practical terms, parent owns model; children observe it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Owner/Observer
keyIdea.text: Parent views should own long-lived models with @StateObject; child views observe them with @ObservedObject to stay in sync.

content.html:
Architecture
ContentView owns GameManager
Parent creates with @StateObject; children declare @ObservedObject to react to changes without owning.
// Parent owns
@StateObject var gameManager = GameManager(name: "Space Invaders")

// Child observes
struct ScoreDisplayView: View {
  @ObservedObject var manager: GameManager
  // displays manager.currentScore
}
Debug tip
Add print in init/deinit to confirm when instances are created or destroyed.
Why it matters
Ownership prevents state resets across navigation and view toggles.
Analogy
Think of @StateObject as the owner holding the model's passport. Observers have a copy of the passport number and can read details, but they don’t control renewal or deletion.

narration.text: Let's step through an implementation you will use in labs. The GameManager class conforms to ObservableObject and uses @Published for currentScore and gameName. The initializer sets defaults and prints a message so you can observe init and deinit in the console. The addScore and resetGame methods mutate currentScore; because currentScore is @Published, these changes automatically notify observing views. Notice how methods are simple and focus on business logic; the view layer subscribes and renders the data. A common confusion is where to put UI code: keep it in SwiftUI views. The model should not import view types or hold references to views. Also watch closures inside GameManager: if you capture self in a repeating timer callback use [weak self] to prevent retain cycles. This code sample is ready to paste into a SwiftUI project for the hands-on activity; it demonstrates initialization, mutation, and predictable notifications, and it is the basis for the parent/child ownership examples you will practice. GameManager code example means keep model logic in observableobject with @published for properties and avoid view references to maintain separation of concerns.. In practical terms, implementing observableobject with @published properties. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Code insight
keyIdea.text: Keep model logic in ObservableObject with @Published for properties and avoid view references to maintain separation of concerns.

content.html:
Code walkthrough
GameManager
A plain ObservableObject implementation you can use in the hands-on activity.
import Combine

class GameManager: ObservableObject {
  @Published var currentScore: Int = 0
  @Published var gameName: String = "My Awesome Game"

  init(initialScore: Int = 0, name: String = "My Awesome Game") {
    self.currentScore = initialScore
    self.gameName = name
    print("GameManager initialized for: \(gameName)")
  }

  deinit {
    print("GameManager deinitialized for: \(gameName)")
  }

  func addScore(_ points: Int) {
    currentScore += points
    print("Score updated to: \(currentScore)")
  }

  func resetGame() {
    currentScore = 0
    print("Game reset.")
  }
}
Example
Create with @StateObject in ContentView and pass to children as @ObservedObject.
Misconception
Don’t mix UI responsibilities into the manager; keep it testable and view-agnostic.
Takeaway
A well-scoped ObservableObject simplifies state sharing and lifecycle control.

screens.title: Lifecycle pitfalls and init/deinit testing
screens.subtitle: Detecting accidental re-creation and data loss

narration.text: A practical way to confirm ownership is to add console logs in your model's initializer and deinitializer. When you expect an instance to persist, the init should fire once and deinit should not fire until the owning view is destroyed. Common lifecycle pitfalls occur when a view initializes an ObservableObject and uses @ObservedObject or when a parent view re-creates a child that also creates a model. In those cases, you will see repeated init messages and possibly deinit messages between renders, indicating state resets. For example, a timer that prints "initialized" each time the view re-renders is a clear sign the view is creating the timer incorrectly. The fix is to move creation to a persistent owner using @StateObject or to keep the instance in an external source. Remember that NavigationView, TabView, and toggling conditional branches can re-create views, so ownership choices must account for these lifecycle events. Use init/deinit logging as a diagnostic step and incorporate unit tests that verify persistence when appropriate. This habit helps you catch bugs early and reason about which view should be the stable owner.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle testing
keyIdea.text: Confirm persistence with init/deinit logs; repeated init indicates accidental re-creation and likely state loss.

content.html:
Lifecycle
Detecting accidental re-creation
Use init/deinit print statements to observe when models are created and destroyed during UI interactions.
init() { print("GameManager initialized") }
deinit { print("GameManager deinitialized") }
What repeated init means
A view is recreating the object on re-evaluation, likely due to incorrect wrapper or placement.
Fix
Move initialization to an owning view using @StateObject or keep a single shared source for the model.
Real-world triggers
  • Parent state changes that re-evaluate child views
  • Navigation push/pop that reconstructs screens
  • Switching tabs that recreate the content view
Takeaway
Logs reveal ownership mistakes; use @StateObject for creators and @ObservedObject for observers.

screens.title: View lifecycle scenarios
screens.subtitle: How NavigationView and TabView affect object persistence

narration.text: Different view containers influence when views are created and destroyed, so your ownership decisions must consider the app structure. In a NavigationView, pushing and popping views can create and destroy screens. If the pushed view owns a model with @StateObject, that model persists for the pushed view's life and deinitializes when the view is popped. In a TabView, switching tabs may keep views alive or rebuild them depending on implementation details, so prefer keeping shared, long-lived models at a higher level using @StateObject in a parent that persists across tab changes. Conditional UI with if/else also recreates views when branches toggle; models created inside the toggled branch must be @StateObject to persist while the branch is active. As a concrete scenario, toggling a ScoreDisplayView inside ContentView should not reset the GameManager if ContentView owns it via @StateObject. The rule of thumb: place long-lived models at the highest stable level that matches their required lifetime, and use @ObservedObject for children that only read or react to shared models. View lifecycle scenarios means choose ownership level based on view container behavior. place long-lived models where they won't be re-created by navigation or tab switches.. In practical terms, how navigationview and tabview affect object persistence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hierarchy rule
keyIdea.text: Choose ownership level based on view container behavior. Place long-lived models where they won't be re-created by navigation or tab switches.

content.html:
Hierarchy
Navigation, tabs, and conditional views
Place models where their lifecycle matches the container behavior to avoid unexpected reinitialization.
NavigationView
Pushed views own models persist while pushed. Pop destroys them.
TabView
Tabs may keep views alive; put shared models in a parent to guarantee persistence across tabs.
Conditional branches
Toggling branches recreates views; owning models should live above transient branches.
Concrete scenario
ContentView owns GameManager with @StateObject. Toggling a child view or switching tabs won't reset the manager because the owner persists at the right level.
Key takeaway
Match model lifetime to a stable parent; that parent should use @StateObject to guarantee persistence.

narration.text: Swift types fall into two categories: value and reference. Value types — structs and enums — are copied when passed around. @State and @Binding work well for these because the view can own simple value-type state safely. Reference types — classes — share a single instance across references. ObservableObject exists because classes require a way to notify views when internal state changes. Use ObservableObject when you need a shared, mutable object that multiple views must observe, or when the model has complex logic and lifecycle. A concrete distinction: a simple Bool or counter used by a single view belongs in @State. A complex GameManager that multiple screens update and read should be a class conforming to ObservableObject with @Published fields. A common misconception is to overuse ObservableObject for data that would be simpler as value types; prefer value types for local, immutable data because they are easier to reason about and test. Keep reference types focused on shared mutable concerns and make ownership explicit with @StateObject to avoid accidental duplication of instances. Reference types vs value types means use value types and @state/@binding for simple local data; use observableobject and @stateobject/@observedobject for shared, complex class-based models.. In practical terms, when to use observableobject over @state/@binding. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Type guidance
keyIdea.text: Use value types and @State/@Binding for simple local data; use ObservableObject and @StateObject/@ObservedObject for shared, complex class-based models.

content.html:
Definition
Reference vs Value
Choose the type that matches your data: copyable value types for local state, classes for shared mutable models.
Value type example
A view's local selection index stored with @State.
Reference type example
GameManager as a shared ObservableObject between parent and children.
Guidance
  • Prefer value types for simple, local state
  • Use ObservableObject for shared mutable data and complex logic
  • Make ownership explicit to avoid duplicate instances
Takeaway
Select types and wrappers based on mutability, sharing needs, and lifetime requirements.

screens.title: Converting @State to ObservableObject
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step migration for a shared model

narration.text: When a piece of state grows beyond a single view, convert it from @State to an ObservableObject in a few clear steps. Step one: extract the state fields and related logic into a new class that conforms to ObservableObject. Step two: mark the properties that the UI should react to with @Published. Step three: in the view that should own the model, replace @State with @StateObject and initialize the class there. Step four: pass the model to child views that need to read or mutate it using @ObservedObject. Step five: test with init/deinit print statements and UI interactions to confirm the object persists across view updates. For example, moving a score counter into GameManager and switching to @StateObject in the parent preserves the score when child views are toggled. Remember to refactor any binding uses — where you previously used $value you may now expose methods or @Published properties on the model. This stepwise migration reduces risk and makes ownership explicit. Converting @State to ObservableObject means extract state into an observableobject, mark @published, create with @stateobject in owner, and pass as @observedobject to children.. In practical terms, step-by-step migration for a shared model. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Incorrect usage

// Toggling parent state may recreate this view and reinit DownloadManager
Symptom

screens.title: Memory safety and objectWillChange
screens.subtitle: Avoid retain cycles and batch updates when needed

narration.text: When working with ObservableObject, two safety themes matter: memory management and update control. Memory leaks often stem from closures that capture self strongly inside an ObservableObject, such as timers or network callbacks. To avoid retain cycles, capture self as weak or unowned depending on lifetime assumptions. For example, in repeating callbacks use [weak self] to avoid holding the object indefinitely. The second theme is update control: @Published ordinarily sends change events for single property updates, but complex state mutations that update multiple properties can produce several sequential renders. To prevent inconsistent intermediate UI states, call objectWillChange. send() once before mutating multiple properties so observers receive a single batched update. A misconception is that @Published always suffices; for atomic multi-property updates explicit signals are sometimes necessary. These patterns keep models robust, avoid memory issues, and produce smoother UI updates in real applications. Memory safety and objectWillChange means use weak captures to prevent retain cycles and objectwillchange.send() to batch multi-property updates when needed.. In practical terms, avoid retain cycles and batch updates when needed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safety rules
keyIdea.text: Use weak captures to prevent retain cycles and objectWillChange.send() to batch multi-property updates when needed.

content.html:
Memory
Avoid retain cycles
When a manager holds a repeating timer or closure, capture self weakly in callbacks to avoid leaks.
timer = Timer.scheduledTimer(withTimeInterval: 1.0, repeats: true) { [weak self] _ in
  self?.tick()
}
Batching
Use objectWillChange for atomic updates
Call objectWillChange.send() before making several related property changes so observers see a single coherent state.
objectWillChange.send()
self.a = newA
self.b = newB
// observers react once with both changes applied
Takeaway
Be deliberate about closure captures and multi-field changes to keep memory and UI stable.

screens.title: Key Concepts — part 1
screens.subtitle: Three core ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize three fundamental concepts you should carry forward. First, ObservableObject and @Published let classes broadcast changes so SwiftUI can update views automatically. Second, @StateObject is the correct choice when a view must create and own a model; it ensures the object is instantiated only once for the view's lifetime. Third, @ObservedObject is for observing models created and owned elsewhere — children should use it when a parent supplies the instance. Each of these concepts maps directly to code and architecture choices: marking properties with @Published, choosing which view initializes the model, and structuring owner and observer relationships across your view hierarchy. Keep these rules in mind when you design components: ownership controls persistence, and correct use prevents subtle bugs like state resets. Ask yourself before creating a model: who must keep it alive? That question guides the wrapper you choose.

ObservableObject
Protocol for classes to notify SwiftUI about changes.
@StateObject
Use when the view creates and must preserve the model instance.
@ObservedObject
Observe an externally owned ObservableObject without managing its lifecycle.
Summary takeaway

Ownership decides persistence: let an owner hold the model with @StateObject and let other views observe it with @ObservedObject.
